rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: The product of oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}\) with \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) in acidic medium is :
rows.solution:
The product is the SULPHATE ion, \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

The question says OXIDATION, so sulphur must move to a HIGHER oxidation state. In the sulphite ion sulphur is \(+4\); in the sulphate ion it is \(+6\), so each sulphur gives up two electrons.

\(5\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 6\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)

Ten electrons change hands: five sulphites give up two each, and two permanganates take five each as manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+2\).

The other three options all move sulphur DOWN — to \(+4\) in sulphur dioxide, to \(-2\) in sulphide, to \(+2\) in thiosulphate. Each would be a REDUCTION, and permanganate is an oxidising agent, so none is possible.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The coordination number of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) is :
rows.solution:
The coordination number of cobalt is SIX.

Coordination number counts DONOR ATOMS attached to the metal, not ligand molecules. Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE: it binds through both of its nitrogens at once, closing a five-membered chelate ring.

Three such ligands therefore supply \(3 \times 2 = 6\) donor atoms, and the complex is octahedral.

Counting the three ligand molecules instead of the six donor atoms gives 3, which is the answer the question is testing for. The distinction matters everywhere a chelating ligand appears — with the hexadentate \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\), a single ligand gives a coordination number of six on its own.

rows.stem: Which one of the following complexes is non-ionisable ?
rows.solution:
The non-ionisable complex is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\).

What ionises in solution is whatever sits OUTSIDE the square brackets. Here the brackets close around all three chlorides: every one of them is a LIGAND bonded directly to cobalt, and there is nothing outside at all.

Check the charges: three ammonia molecules are neutral and three chlorido ligands give \(-3\), so with cobalt at \(+3\) the complex is NEUTRAL overall — nothing is needed outside to balance it, and nothing is there.

The other three all carry counter ions and ionise accordingly, into 2, 3 and 4 ions respectively. The difference is measurable: a conductivity measurement distinguishes the four at once, and that is exactly how Werner established their structures.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a benzylic halide ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR options are PRINTED AS DRAWINGS and the stem names nothing. Each is a skeletal Kekule benzene ring (three inner double-bond strokes, verified at 2.6x) carrying: (A) a two-carbon chain "CH2 - CH2 - X"; (B) "X" at one vertex and "CH3" at the ADJACENT vertex; (C) a central "C" bonded to "X" with a "CH3" above and a "CH3" below; (D) a chain "CH2 - CH - CH3" with "X" hanging below the middle carbon. Transcribed above as the equivalent condensed formulae, which preserve the discrimination the question tests. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The benzylic halide is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}C(CH_3)_2{-}X}\).

A BENZYLIC halide has its halogen on the \(sp^3\) carbon ATTACHED DIRECTLY to the benzene ring. Here that carbon carries the ring, two methyl groups and the halogen — it is benzylic, and tertiary besides.

The others fail on position or on kind. In \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}X}\) the halogen is one carbon TOO FAR from the ring; in \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH(X){-}CH_3}\) it is likewise on the second carbon. And \(o\)-\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}X}\) has its halogen ON the ring itself, which makes it an ARYL halide — a class at the opposite extreme of reactivity.

The position matters because a benzylic carbocation is stabilised by resonance with the ring, which is why benzylic halides are unusually reactive while aryl halides are unusually inert.

Phenol is less acidic than o-NITROPHENOL.

Acidity here is decided by what the substituent does to the PHENOXIDE ion left behind after the proton leaves. An electron-WITHDRAWING group helps disperse the negative charge, stabilises the anion and strengthens the acid; an electron-RELEASING group does the reverse.

The nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing, both inductively and by resonance, so o-nitrophenol is markedly STRONGER than phenol — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 7.2 against 10.

The other three are all weaker than phenol. Methoxy and methyl groups both RELEASE electron density into the ring, destabilising the anion. Ethanol is weaker by a wide margin — about \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 16 — because an alkoxide ion has no ring to delocalise its charge into at all.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\,C - O - CH_3}\) reacts with HI to give :
rows.solution:
The products are tert-BUTYL IODIDE AND METHANOL, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}I} + \mathrm{CH_3OH}\).

Cleaving an ether with hydrogen iodide breaks whichever bond gives the easier route, and here one side is TERTIARY. The protonated ether can simply fall apart to a tertiary carbocation — stabilised by three methyl groups — which the iodide then captures. So the reaction takes the UNIMOLECULAR route, the iodine goes to the tertiary carbon, and the methyl group keeps the oxygen.

\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}I} + \mathrm{CH_3OH}\)

Had BOTH groups been primary the mechanism would have been bimolecular, and the iodide would have attacked the LESS hindered carbon instead — giving the opposite pairing. Which bond breaks is decided by the mechanism, and the mechanism by the substitution.

rows.stem: Aspirin is formed by the acetylation of :
rows.solution:
Aspirin is formed by acetylating SALICYLIC ACID.

Salicylic acid carries both a carboxyl group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent ring carbons. Acetic anhydride acetylates the HYDROXYL, leaving the carboxyl free:
\(\mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3COO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is acetylsalicylic acid — aspirin.

The point of the acetylation is medical rather than chemical. Free salicylic acid irritates the stomach lining badly; masking its phenolic hydroxyl as an ester makes the drug tolerable, and the ester is hydrolysed back in the body.

rows.stem: An azeotropic solution of two liquids has boiling point higher than either of them when it :

options.label: B
options.text: shows positive deviation from Raoult's law

options.label: C
options.text: shows negative deviation from Raoult's law

options.label: D
options.text: shows no deviation from Raoult's law

rows.solution:
An azeotrope boiling higher than either component shows a NEGATIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

In a negative deviation the vapour pressure of the solution is LOWER than predicted, because the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are STRONGER than those between like ones, so the molecules escape less readily.

Lower vapour pressure means a HIGHER boiling point — the mixture must be heated further before it reaches atmospheric pressure — and the azeotrope is a maximum boiling one. Nitric acid with water is the standard case, boiling at 393.5 K at about 68% acid, higher than either pure liquid.

Positive deviation does the reverse and gives a MINIMUM boiling azeotrope, while a solution with no deviation is ideal and forms no azeotrope at all.

COPPER IS FORMED AT THE CATHODE.

The cathode is where reduction happens, and the two candidates are the copper ion and water:
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\), \(E^{\circ} = +0{\cdot}34\) V
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\), \(E^{\circ} = -0{\cdot}83\) V

The species with the HIGHER reduction potential is reduced preferentially, and \(+0{\cdot}34\) is far higher, so copper is deposited and no hydrogen appears. This is the basis of electroplating and of electrolytic refining.

At the ANODE chlorine is evolved, not oxygen — liberating oxygen carries a substantial OVERPOTENTIAL that wipes out its small thermodynamic advantage. So the oxygen option is wrong, and the chlorine option is wrong only in naming the electrode.

Contrast this with sodium chloride solution, where the metal ion's potential is far too negative and water is reduced instead.

rows.stem: Half-life period of a first order reaction is 1386 seconds. The rate constant (k) of the reaction is :
rows.solution:
For a FIRST ORDER reaction the half-life is related to the rate constant by
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)

Rearranging and substituting:
\(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{1386} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

that is \(0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

The unit is a check on the working: a first order constant must come out as reciprocal time, and it does.

The distinguishing feature of first order is that this half-life contains NO concentration term at all — the time to fall by half is the same whatever concentration it starts from, which is why the question can quote it as a single number.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of the reaction \(2\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{AB}\) is given by
\(\text{Rate} = \mathrm{k}\,[\mathrm{A}]^2\,[\mathrm{B_2}]\).
The value of rate constant (k) can be increased by :
rows.solution:
The rate constant can be increased only by INCREASING THE TEMPERATURE.

The rate and the rate CONSTANT are different quantities, and this question turns on that difference. Concentration moves the rate; it does not move the constant.

By the Arrhenius equation
\(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\)
the constant depends on the temperature, on the activation energy and on the nature of the reaction — and on nothing else. No concentration term appears in it anywhere.

So raising \([\mathrm{A}]\) or \([\mathrm{B_2}]\) would raise the RATE, exactly as the given rate law says, while leaving \(k\) untouched. Raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules carrying the activation energy, and that does change \(k\).

Adding a catalyst would change it too, by lowering \(E_a\) — but that is not among the choices.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aromatic primary amines can be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Alkyl halide undergoes nucleophilic substitution with anion formed by phthalimide.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Gabriel phthalimide synthesis cannot make AROMATIC primary amines. Its key step is a nucleophilic substitution in which the phthalimide anion displaces halide from an ALKYL halide — and an ARYL halide will not undergo that substitution at all, its carbon-halogen bond having partial double bond character from resonance with the ring.

The Reason is correct and describes exactly that step: potassium hydroxide removes phthalimide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, and the anion so formed attacks the alkyl halide.

So the Reason states precisely the reason the Assertion fails — the method depends on a reaction that aryl halides do not undergo. Aniline is made instead by reducing nitrobenzene.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Uracil base is present in RNA.
Reason (R) : RNA undergoes self-replication.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Uracil IS present in RNA. Both nucleic acids carry adenine, guanine and cytosine, but the fourth base differs: RNA has uracil where DNA has thymine. So the Assertion holds.

The Reason does not. It is DNA that undergoes self-replication, each strand serving as the template for its complement. RNA is SYNTHESISED FROM DNA rather than replicating itself, and its work is to direct the synthesis of proteins.

The two statements are unrelated in any case: which base occupies the fourth slot has no bearing on whether the molecule can replicate.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diazonium salts of aliphatic amines are more stable than those of aromatic amines.
Reason (R) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines show resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

The stability runs the other way. AROMATIC diazonium salts are the more stable — benzenediazonium chloride survives at 273-278 K and can even be isolated as a solid — whereas an ALIPHATIC diazonium salt breaks up the moment it forms, with brisk effervescence of nitrogen.

The Reason is correct: an aromatic diazonium ion IS stabilised by resonance, its positive charge delocalised into the benzene ring. An aliphatic one has no ring to spread the charge over.

So the Reason states exactly why the Assertion is false. Corrected — aromatic salts being the more stable — it would have explained the Assertion perfectly; as written the Assertion names the wrong compound.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Acetanilide \((\mathrm{C_6H_5 - NHCOCH_3})\) is less basic than aniline.
Reason (R) : Acetylation of aniline results in decrease of electron density on nitrogen in acetanilide.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — the Assertion prints acetanilide as a MIXED inline structure: a small skeletal Kekule benzene ring drawn inside the parentheses, bonded to the typeset label "NHCOCH3". Transcribed above as the equivalent condensed formula, which is a lossless reading and gives nothing away (the compound is already NAMED in the same sentence). Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Acetanilide is much the weaker base of the two, and the Reason gives the cause exactly.

Acetylating the nitrogen puts a CARBONYL group beside it, and that carbonyl withdraws the nitrogen's lone pair onto its own oxygen by resonance. With less electron density on nitrogen there is less available to accept a proton, so the amide is the weaker base. Aniline's lone pair is delocalised only into the ring, which is a gentler pull.

The effect has a practical use. Acetylation MODERATES the amino group's activating power, which is why an aniline must be acetylated before it can be mono-brominated — without that protection, bromine water gives the tribromo product at once.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Essential amino acids
(b) Nucleotide
rows.solution:
(a) ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS are those the body CANNOT synthesise for itself; they have to be supplied in the diet. Valine, leucine, isoleucine and lysine are among them.

The contrast is with NON-ESSENTIAL amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, which the body can make. Note that the name describes what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis, and a protein cannot be built if any one residue is missing.

(b) A NUCLEOTIDE is a nucleoside joined to PHOSPHORIC ACID — in other words, a unit made of three parts: a nitrogenous BASE, a pentose SUGAR and a PHOSPHATE group.

The parts join in a fixed order. The base attaches to \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the sugar, and that two-part unit is a NUCLEOSIDE; the phosphate then esterifies the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\), making it a nucleotide. It is the phosphate that links one sugar to the next, so nucleotides are the units from which a nucleic acid chain is built.

rows.stem:
(a) In the following pair of compounds, which compound undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction faster and why ?
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5 - CH_2Cl}\) OR \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11} - CH_2Cl}\)
(b) Write the major product in the following :
Cyclohexene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2},\ \text{UV light}}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — BOTH sub-parts are printed as DRAWINGS, and the ring type IS the discrimination. ⚠ This typesetter distinguishes three ring kinds and all three appear on this page; each was verified at 10x. (a) prints the pair as two hexagons joined by the word OR, each bonded to the label "CH2Cl": the LEFT hexagon carries THREE inner double-bond strokes (a Kekule benzene ring), the RIGHT hexagon carries NO inner strokes at all (a saturated cyclohexane ring) — so the pair is benzyl chloride versus cyclohexylmethyl chloride, transcribed above as the equivalent condensed formulae. (b) prints a hexagon carrying exactly ONE inner stroke parallel to its left edge — i.e. ONE double bond, CYCLOHEXENE, neither benzene nor cyclohexane — followed by a long reaction arrow labelled "Br2 , UV light" with no product shown. The reading is corroborated by the official marking scheme (ms p02), which answers (i) with a drawn benzyl chloride and (ii) with 3-bromocyclohexene, an allylic bromination that is only correct for an alkene. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) BENZYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2Cl}\), reacts faster.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step — so the question is which cation is the more stable.

The benzyl cation is stabilised by RESONANCE: its positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, over the ortho and para positions. The cyclohexylmethyl cation from \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}CH_2Cl}\) has a saturated ring beside it and no such delocalisation; it remains a plain primary carbocation.

The two look alike on paper — both are primary halides attached to a six-membered ring — and the whole difference lies in whether that ring is aromatic.

(b) Bromine on cyclohexene under ULTRAVIOLET LIGHT is not an addition at all. Those conditions generate bromine RADICALS, and a radical abstracts a hydrogen rather than adding to the double bond. It takes the one most easily abstracted — the ALLYLIC hydrogen on the carbon next to the double bond — because the radical left behind is delocalised over the double bond.

Major product: 3-BROMOCYCLOHEXENE, the ring keeping its double bond with \(\mathrm{Br}\) on the adjacent carbon.

In the dark, bromine would simply add across the double bond to give the 1,2-dibromide instead.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A 4% solution of urea (molar mass = 60 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) is isotonic with \(5{\cdot}2\%\) solution of an unknown organic substance. Calculate the molecular weight of the unknown organic substance.
rows.solution:
ISOTONIC means the two solutions have the SAME osmotic pressure. Since \(\Pi = CRT\) and both are at the same temperature, equal osmotic pressure means equal MOLAR CONCENTRATION:
\(C_{\text{urea}} = C_{\mathrm{A}}\)

Both percentages are mass per unit volume and refer to the same volume, so the concentrations may be compared as mass divided by molar mass:
\(\dfrac{w_{\text{urea}}}{M_{\text{urea}}} = \dfrac{w_{\mathrm{A}}}{M_{\mathrm{A}}}\)
\(\dfrac{4}{60} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}2}{M_{\mathrm{A}}}\)

\(M_{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}2 \times 60}{4} = 5{\cdot}2 \times 15\)

\(M_{\mathrm{A}} = 78\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The result is worth a sanity check: the unknown is present at a GREATER mass than the urea yet gives the same number of moles, so its molar mass must be the larger of the two — and 78 exceeds 60, as it should. Note also that neither answer depends on knowing the temperature, since it cancels on both sides.
